highlights.title: The Nvidia Shield TV Is 7 Years Old. It Just Got a $100 Price Hike
highlights.summary: The price of anything with memory is skyrocketing thanks to AI. Aging streaming devices are no exception.
body: The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.

The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.

Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
points: The price of anything with memory is skyrocketing thanks to AI.
The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive.

Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers.

NDAs are a significant piece of the broader data center backlash. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich recently said that the number one complaint she’s heard about data centers is transparency, with these projects following a common pattern: “projects announced after permits are already secured, developers who don’t return calls, local officials who signed NDAs before their neighbors knew a project was being considered.”

highlights.title: India win Asian Games - but denied ODI sweep over West Indies by superb Hope
highlights.summary: India beat Pakistan in T20 cricket to secure back-to-back gold medals at the Asian Games - but their ODI side were unable to complete a 3-0 sweep of West Indies on the same day after Shai Hope's 162 not out led the tourists to their record chase of 352.
body: In the Asian Games final in Japan, India smoked 211-6 from their 20 overs, underpinned by Abhishek Sharma's 61 off 28 balls, Tilak Varma's 51 not out from 22 and Shivam Dube's 27 off 15.
Pakistan plummeted to 39-3 in reply and despite Hasan Nawaz's 96 off 51 balls, they could muster only 192-6 and lost by 19 runs.
The victory was India's seventh in a row over Pakistan in T20Is and their 14th in the 18 matches between the teams in the format.

In New Chandigarh, however, India saw their total of 351-7 eclipsed by West Indies with 10 balls to spare as visiting captain Hope struck his 21st ODI hundred and second in as many matches to secure a five-wicket win after defeats in Thiruvananthapuram and Guwahati.

highlights.title: The 8 Best Games Like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
highlights.summary: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is one of, if not the best, RPGs of all time. 11 years after launch, everyone's playing it again thanks to a fancy new remaster (that's free for anyone who owns the existing game), meant to prep players for the Songs of the Past expansion that's in the works.
body: The Witcher 3 has plenty of defining traits: a beautiful, dense open world; side quests with narratives so enrapturing they're better than most games' main stories; larger-than-life characters who become so personable, you'd consider them friends; and combat mechanics that allow you to dance between foes, all while using two swords and magic at once.
If any of that sounds like your sort of thing, here are the eight best games like The Witcher 3.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is the newest game on this list, and it comes from studio Rebel Wolves, which is led by The Witcher 3 game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz. The studio also employs a number of other former high-level staffers from CD Projekt Red, and as a result, it's one of the closest games you'll find to matching what Geralt's best adventure has to offer.

In The Blood of Dawnwalker, you are Coen. He's part-vampire, part-witch, a.k.a. a Dawnwalker. Not a Witcher. Structurally, however, this is heavily inspired by The Witcher games: a stunning open world with so many side quests to find, innovative, direction-based, parry-focused combat, and a unique time-based mechanic where every decision truly matters.
points: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is one of, if not the best, RPGs of all time.

Special Effect provides assessments and customised technology loans to help physically disabled people play games, and takes what it learns back to hardware and software developers to help make their products more accessible. Thousands of disabled people ask for the charity’s help every year.

highlights.title: Ace Combat 8 Secretly Has the Best Video Game Music of the Year
highlights.summary: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is one of the best video games I’ve played in 2026, and there are plenty of reasons why. It has airtight flying controls, features a diversity of thrilling missions, revitalizes a series that’s been silent for years, and happens to be one of the best-looking games of…
body: That claim will only come as a surprise if you’re not familiar with the Ace Combat series. Long-time fans have always known that the Ace Combat series’ music is one of its best qualities. That’s thanks in part to composer Keiki Kobayashi, whose soaring orchestral compositions give the series’ aerial missions a sense of grandeur. This time around, Kobayashi worked alongside Ryo Watanabe and Mitsuhiro Kitadani to create the series’ best score yet.
Don’t take it from me. Take six minutes to listen to the game’s main theme, “Everflow.” Though be warned that it will make you feel like you can run through a wall.

The word “epic” gets overused a lot in video game culture, but it’s really the only way to describe the compositions in Ace Combat 8. Each one feels enormous in scope, filled with choirs that feel impossibly large and string sections that drag a bow across your heart. They get your blood pumping during tense missions, but they also are emotionally charged enough to add some real weight to the war you’re fighting. It evokes the blockbuster sounds of the Metal Gear Solid soundtrack.
points: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is one of the best video games I’ve played in 2026, and there are plenty of reasons why.

highlights.title: Video Games Europe hits back at EU watchdog targeting King, Supercell, Mojang and more over IAP practices
highlights.summary: The EU’s Consumer Protection Cooperation Network has launched coordinated enforcement actions against games companies including King, Supercell, Mojang, Riot Games, Activision Blizzard and Ubisoft, over how they sell and handle in-game virtual currencies.
body: The CPC Network brings together national consumer protection authorities from across the EU and EEA and is coordinated by the European Commission. In a joint statement published September 30, it said it had found that “a high number of video game companies” had made no substantive changes to their practices since it published non-binding “Key Principles” on in-game currencies in March 2025, despite extensive subsequent talks with industry bodies.

It said the coordinated actions are particularly focused on compliance around variable reward systems such as loot boxes, “dark patterns” and other “harmful influencing techniques”, and practices that directly exhort children to spend money, which it says EU law already prohibits.
Video Games Europe and the European Game Developers Federation pushed back on the CPC Network’s actions in a statement also published on September 30.

And we have gone deeper: asking a food lab to test the best non-toxic pans, blind-tasting everything from protein bars to nonalcoholic beer and getting the tea on Padma Lakshmi’s favorite kitchen tools. Across hundreds of articles, we have covered everything from a satisfyingly bouncy $1,600 organic mattress to a small but mighty $9 cleaning brush. We have found the legitimately best deals on our favorite things too.

One year in, we wanted to know which things should earn a permanent place in your homes. So we pulled the 25 items our readers have loved most since the Filter US launched – then went back to the writers who originally tested them. Did the products survive months of real life? Would our testers still recommend them to you?

highlights.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Video Reveals Major Change That Could End Wallhacks for Good
highlights.summary: Wallhacks have plagued Call of Duty for years, but in Modern Warfare 4, Activision has a plan to change that. If you're unfamiliar with the term, wallhacks are a type of cheat that allows nefarious players to see their opponents' every move through walls.
body: As detailed in a new video published on the franchise's official social media pages, publisher Activision and developer Infinity Ward revealed a new system aimed at combating wallhack cheaters. Called "server culling," the goal is to make Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 more reliable – and fair – than ever before.

The relatively in-depth explanation touches on how cheaters have been able to use wallhacks thus far. Usually, servers share information, such as a player's in-game location, between game clients. It means that, even when you can't see an enemy hiding behind cover, waiting to pop out for an easy kill, the game itself still recognizes that the player is there.

Server culling, which saw Infinity Ward build occlusion layers into Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's environments, essentially limits information to what the player is able to see. So, if you can't see someone behind the wall, the backend can't either – and that goes for wallhackers, too.
"For legitimate players, the match plays exactly as intended," Activision explained. "For cheat developers, this creates a major new obstacle."

highlights.title: Jerry Golod, Producer of ‘Tales From the Darkside’ and Former CBS And NBC Executive, Dies at 87
highlights.summary: Jerry Golod, the producer of “Tales From the Darkside,” died following a brief battle with cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif., on Wednesday. He was 87. Throughout his career, Golod served as an executive at CBS and NBC, later launching JayGee Productions in the early 1980s.
body: In 1975, Golod became vice president of children’s programs at CBS before moving to NBC Entertainment in 1979 as vice president and national program director. While there, he oversaw daytime and children’s programming, specials, variety and West Coast late-night programming. He later joined CBS Television Studios and The CW in developing a new revival of “Tales From the Darkside,” though the series never moved past a 2015 pilot.

Golod executive produced CBS’s “Brass” in 1985 and “Return to Green Acres,” which reunited cast members of the 1960s sitcom. He also executive produced the 1991 revival of “Land of the Lost,” which ran for two seasons.

Golod was born in the Bronx on Dec. 26, 1938, and graduated from City College of New York. He began his career at advertising agency Dancer Fitzgerald Sample and went on to become vice president and associate director of programming. He also spent three years overseeing a television production company affiliated with the agency.
In the ‘90s, Golod worked with Pet Television Network as co-chairman and co-owner of a cable and satellite service aimed toward animal enthusiasts.

highlights.title: My relationship with food was broken. Then I killed my own dinner
highlights.summary: For years, eating was something to control, fear or regret. After I hunted my first deer, I started to see fat, hunger and my own body in a different light. I muffled my sobs with a pillow so my family couldn’t hear me from the adjacent room.
body: Pulling tear-soaked strands of hair off my cheeks, I stood in front of a full-length mirror and grabbed the fat of my thighs. If only I could just – I pictured ripping off fistfuls of my body and flinging them out the windows, where they would land on some unknowing French person six stories below. I had this vision often: pulling bits of myself off and casting them somewhere far away from me.

For years, spanning my teens and 20s, eating was either an indulgence to regret or a strategy to overplan. In high school, I chugged 32 ounces of cold green tea every morning, hoping it would burn belly fat like Instagram told me it would. While working at a deli one summer, I ate two bagel sandwiches each shift until my friend mentioned I was eating the carbohydrate equivalent of 10 slices of bread. My daily bagel intake promptly plummeted to zero. I forced myself to choke down a can of tuna in my college dorm before predawn weightlifting sessions. In my early 20s, I started experimenting with intermittent fasting: no food from 8pm until noon the next day.
points: For years, eating was something to control, fear or regret.

highlights.title: Computational tools for society’s most complex challenges
highlights.summary: Associate Professor Cathy Wu uses reinforcement learning to help map out improvements to transportation and other multifaceted systems.
body: As far back as she can remember, Cathy Wu ’12, MNG ’13 wanted to find ways to solve problems to improve people’s lives. Her parents were Taiwanese immigrants, and her father had a long commute to his job, which took him away from the family. On a tight budget, the rest of the family often stayed home on a street that was too busy for playing outdoors. Wu and her siblings ended up playing a lot of computer games.

Wu says her desire to make the world a better place, her dad’s daily battle against traffic, and the games she played, like “SimCity,” were the seeds of her motivation to design safe, efficient transportation systems.

Wu is an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Her research focuses on using machine learning and reinforcement learning (RL) to advance reliable strategies for improving a range of complex systems, including transportation.

body: Speaking to Radio Times, as spotted by IGN, Hamaguchi explained his own attachment to physical media, from buying games as a child to wanting friends and colleagues in the industry to sign copies of their work.

"Personally, obviously, I bought lots of physical editions of games as a child. Sometimes I buy digital editions of games, but if I'm particularly attached to a title, I want to get the physical version," he said, adding that the topic has become "particularly sensitive" in recent months.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will ship with a disc option when it launches in 2027, but PS5 and Xbox Series X players popping in a physical copy will still need to download a hefty chunk of the game to play it in full.
Hamaguchi acknowledged the disc included is a "key disc" containing only the game's opening, and that he understands why some fans have said "no disc, no purchase".

highlights.summary: Dropout CEO Sam Reich chats with Polygon about lessons he's learned from eight seasons of Game Changer and how the Topeka trip almost didn't happen.
body: For a moment, Dropout CEO and Game Changer host Sam Reich wondered if he could get away with not going to Topeka, Kansas.

The Game Changer season 8 episode “What’s the Catch” starts as if the episode is all about handing out prizes, but those prizes quickly get a “catch” that turns them into punishments. At one point, one of contestant Jacob Wysocki’s “prizes” turns into a private improv show where Sam drives him around. Eventually, it gets the catch of having to take place in Topeka, Kansas, and suddenly the tormentor also becomes the tormented. Reich and Wysocki are forced on a trip to Topeka for the most random improv show inside their rented car.
“There was a moment between Jacob and I after the fact where we talked about faking it,” Reich tells Polygon.
Dropout considered just pretending to go to Kansas for the bit, but worried that the Game Changer audience would know. Ultimately, Reich decided not to go down that path.

highlights.summary: As a fan of Henri Cartier-Bresson, the Egyptian photographer was determined to capture his own ‘decisive moment’ Mirna Abass regards his small Egyptian city as “heaven for street, travel and documentary photography”.
body: On the day he took this shot, Abass had joined a walk with the Egyptian Camera Crew photography club. Abass works as an agricultural engineer, but describes film and photography as his true passions. Henri Cartier-Bresson is one of his biggest inspirations, and he is often guided by the pioneering photographer’s concept of the decisive moment.

“As we explored the shipyard, I saw this teenage fisher jumping between several boats,” Abass says. “I set up my iPhone 13 to capture these two contrasting boats, side by side, and waited patiently, hoping he might eventually make the jump in front of me. I was elated when he did, and went to show him our very own decisive moment.

“The human element gave a sense of scale, of how large these ships are, and I loved how I captured him leaping from the white ship to the colourful ship,” he adds. “It is almost as if he is escaping from pale life to fruitful life.”

highlights.title: An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm
highlights.summary: David Robinson used to write the safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI. This week, he resigned from his position and is now speaking out in an editorial in The Atlantic.
body: It’s understandable if you’re feeling a bit cynical about everyone suddenly coming out of the woodwork to warn about how dangerous the thing they helped build is. They did, after all, make this mess. But that doesn’t mean we should discount their warnings.

Robinson says that the culture in industry is fundamentally broken. That this is a deeper issue than simply slapping a few new rules or regulations on how we handle training models. Silicon Valley has operated with “extreme confidence” and “perpetual sprints,” he says, building bigger and better models with “unimpeded optimism” that ignores or underestimates potential problems.

Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.

highlights.title: Asghar Farhadi Says Films Like ‘Argo’ Perpetuate American White Savior Myth: ‘Who Asked You To Come and Save Us?’
highlights.summary: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Twice Oscar-winning filmmaker Asghar Farhadi, who is at the Rio Film Festival to present “Parallel Tales,” spoke about the perceived hegemony of American cinema and how Hollywood shouldn’t be seen as a source for faithful portrayals of foreign cultures.
body: Asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A Separation” won Best International Film at the Oscars, Farhadi said he watched the film at the time it came out and felt it was a “Hollywood thing.” In the film, loosely based on a true story, director Ben Affleck plays a Latino exfiltration specialist who masquerades as a Hollywood producer to rescue six Americans held captive in Tehran during the U.S. hostage crisis in Iran. The moderator mentioned how Affleck’s film portrays Iran “like you’re in hell.”

Farhadi then recalled spending time in the U.S. a few years ago when working on a project and, during research, travelling to San Francisco to speak with incarcerated men. “I met some people in prison who are Black, [some who come] from other countries, and the real America was there. But people in the world don’t see that part of the United States.”

“I have this problem when they feel they are up and they think, ‘[others] should be like us,’” he continued. “Even if it’s in a good way and they want to be kind to you, they wish ‘one day you’ll become like us,’ and no, I don’t want to.”

The space is open to the public, maintained as a non-profit working space, and has tools and teaching for 3D printing, laser cutters, CNCs, woodshop tools, knitting and…
We learned about meshnet and meshcore decentralized networking, hacking hardware, and just doing cool things with technology while visiting.
Visit Noisebridge at 272 Capp St, San Francisco, CA 94110.
